extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties in TTAB inter partes trademark proceedings (practitioners before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing discovery conduct in inter partes proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, including conferences, disclosures, searches, supplementation, filing, and motions. Covers obligations under 37 CFR § 2.120 and applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure provisions (notably Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 and 37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to Conduct Discovery Conference (408.01(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties in inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, are required to hold a conference to discuss settlement and plans for discovery, including the nature and basis of the involved claims and defenses, the possibility of settlement or modification of the pleadings, and plans for disclosures and discovery, as well as the subjects set forth in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f) and any other subjects that the Board requires to be discussed in the institution order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to promote cooperation, settlement, efficient adjudication, and discussion of alternative case resolution (e.g., Accelerated Case Resolution). Parties may discuss additional topics but mere discussion of settlement does not substitute for a full discovery conference addressing Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 and the Board's institution order. All parties have a duty to cooperate and conduct the discovery conference timely. If a party refuses to cooperate, the scheduling party should contact the assigned Board attorney; the Board may set a date, warn nonparticipating parties, and consider sanctions under 37 CFR § 2.120(g) (including judgment). A motion to compel participation is not a prerequisite to moving for sanctions, but the moving party must provide evidence of a good faith effort to schedule the conference. See cited authority (Promgirl, Guthy-Renker, etc.) and TBMP cross-references (e.g., TBMP § 401.01, § 528.05(a)(2), § 702.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to Make Initial and Expert Testimony Disclosures (408.01(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party is obliged to make initial disclosures and, when necessary, expert testimony disclosures as part of the discovery phase of inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007. Initial disclosures must be made by the deadline in the Board's institution order; expert disclosures must be served 30 days prior to the close of discovery pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective is early exchange of information to promote settlement, efficient discovery and trial, reduce unfair surprise, and provide basic information about a party's claims/defenses (names of potential witnesses, basic document information). Expert disclosures can be extensive and generally should not be filed with the Board, but the party should notify the Board when an expert disclosure is made so the Board can issue appropriate orders (for example, suspension to allow expert discovery). Parties are encouraged to stipulate to more expansive reciprocal disclosures and are expected to discuss the use of experts at the discovery conference and revisit this as needed. See TBMP § 401.02, § 401.03, and notes/cases (e.g., General Council of the Assemblies of God v. Heritage Music Foundation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Cooperate With Regard to Written Discovery and Disclosures / Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) Certification (408.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: By signing, an attorney or party certifies that, to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief formed after a reasonable inquiry: (A) with respect to a disclosure, it is complete and correct as of the time it is made; and (B) with respect to a discovery request, response, or objection, it is (i) consistent with the rules and warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument to change law, (ii) not interposed for an improper purpose (harass, delay, increase cost), and (iii) neither unreasonable nor unduly burdensome or expensive considering the needs of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The signature constitutes a certification and violations may result in sanctions (per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(g) and TBMP § 106.02). The duty requires a reasonable factual inquiry. Because a signature certifies that a request is warranted, a party ordinarily cannot claim propriety for its own requests but impropriety when propounded by an adversary absent persuasive reasons. Prior to filing a motion to compel disclosure or discovery, the moving party must make a good faith effort by conference or correspondence to resolve the dispute; a written statement showing such a good faith effort must support the motion (37 CFR § 2.120(e)). The Board may require parties to confer with the Board attorney before filing a motion to compel. See cases cited (Miss America Pageant v. Petite Productions; International Finance Corp. v. Bravo Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Search Records (408.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party served with a request for discovery must thoroughly search its records for all information properly sought and provide such information within the time allowed. For document production, a proper response must state that responsive documents exist and will be produced or withheld on a claim of privilege; state an objection with reasons; or state that no responsive documents exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For electronically stored information (ESI), if no form is specified or the party objects, the response should state the form the party intends to use (Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(D)). Responding parties must select and produce the items requested and avoid 'dumping' large quantities of unrequested materials. An incomplete search that produces an incomplete response may preclude the responding party from relying at trial on information properly sought but not produced (unless timely supplemented under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e) and the requesting party raises the issue). Estoppel sanctions have been applied where appropriate (see cited cases, e.g., No Fear Inc. v. Rule; Panda Travel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Supplement Disclosures and Discovery Responses (408.03 / Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who has made a disclosure or responded to interrogatories, requests for production, or requests for admission must supplement or correct its disclosure or response in a timely manner if it learns that in some material respect the disclosure or response is incomplete or incorrect and the additional or corrective information has not otherwise been made known during discovery, or as ordered by the court. For experts, the duty extends to information in the report and given at deposition; additions/changes must be disclosed by the time of pretrial disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board proceedings follow Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e)(1) and (2). There is no obligation to amend prior responses if the information has been made known to the propounding party during discovery (e.g., in a deposition). Parties should not withhold material items to disclose at the last minute; such conduct may risk preclusion under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1). However, prompt supplementation while discovery remains open typically avoids exclusion of testimony (Board policy favors cure where supplementation is timely or deficiencies are promptly remedied). Parties will not be sanctioned for failing to provide ESI lost as a result of routine, good-faith operation of an electronic information system. The Board may also impose a supplementation duty by order. See notes and cases (e.g., Spier Wines; Great Seats; Galaxy Metal Gear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Discovery Requests, Responses, and Disclosures With the Board (37 CFR § 2.120(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery requests, responses, materials or depositions obtained through discovery, and initial and expert disclosures should not be filed with the Board except when submitted with a motion relating to disclosure or discovery, in support of or response to a motion for summary judgment, under a notice of reliance when permitted during a party's testimony period, or as exhibits to a testimony deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should generally not file copies of documents/information disclosed to adversaries (including expert disclosures) but should file a notice that such a disclosure has been made when appropriate so the Board may suspend proceedings for expert-related discovery. Pretrial disclosures are not discovery period disclosures and need not be filed unless a motion to strike is filed. When objecting to proffered evidence or moving to strike testimony on grounds that required discovery/disclosures were not provided, the objecting party should submit copies of the pertinent discovery request(s) and response(s) or disclosures in support of the objection or motion. See 37 CFR § 2.120(j)(6), (8) and cited cases (Hiraga; Life Zone; Ballet Tech; Tri-Star; Kohler; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Discovery Materials at Testimony (37 CFR § 2.120(j)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (j) will not be interpreted to preclude reading or use of written disclosures or documents, a discovery deposition, or answer to an interrogatory, or admission as part of the examination or cross-examination of any witness during the testimony period of any party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery depositions, interrogatory answers, and admissions may be used during witness examination or cross-examination in the testimony period. However, there are limitations on what discovery-originated materials may be made of record by notice of reliance (e.g., printed publications and official records, and certain produced admissions/depositions). Case law clarifies admissibility and permissible methods of making discovery materials of record; see notes/cases (Hiraga; Life Zone; ProQuest; Kohler; B.V.D. Licensing; Genesco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asserting Objections to Discovery and Motions Attacking Requests (410)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules permit assertion of objections to discovery requests believed improper and provide methods for testing sufficiency (motion to compel for depositions/interrogatories/requests for production; motion to test sufficiency of answers or objections for requests for admission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party failing to respond within the allowed time and unable to show excusable neglect may be found, upon motion to compel, to have forfeited its right to object to the discovery. Motions challenging discovery must be supported by a written statement that a good faith effort (conference or correspondence) was made to resolve issues before seeking Board intervention (see 37 CFR § 2.120(e)). The Board has case law demonstrating application of sanctions and restrictions where objections are improper, boilerplate, or where parties fail to cooperate (see cited cases in the chapter).
